title: Before God Changed Their Story, He Changed What They Were Called
paragraphs: Before God Changed Their Story, He Changed What They Were Called
Abram became Abraham. Jacob became Israel. Simon became Cephas. And hidden inside those changed names is a terrifyingly beautiful truth about what Jesus can do with the name your past gave you.
There is a name people know you by.
And then there is the name your pain whispers when nobody is around.
Failure.
Addict.
Rejected.
Unwanted.
Divorced.
Dirty.
Hypocrite.
Not enough.
Too far gone.
Maybe nobody has ever actually called you that.
They didn't have to.
Some names are never spoken aloud.
They are carved into the soul by what happened to us, what was done to us, what we did to others, and what we did when we thought nobody was watching.
And after hearing them long enough, something frightening happens.
We stop believing they describe something we did...
and start believing they describe who we are.
That is why there is something breathtaking hidden in the moments when God changes someone's name in Scripture.

God does not arbitrarily rename every person He transforms. Moses remained Moses. David remained David. Paul is often misunderstood here too: Scripture does not actually describe God formally changing Saul's name to Paul; Acts 13:9 simply identifies him as “Saul, who was also called Paul.”
So this is not a formula.
It is something richer.
In certain decisive moments of the biblical story, a changed name becomes a visible sign that God is declaring covenant, destiny, calling, or transformed identity over a human life.
And sometimes God speaks that new reality while the person's story still looks nothing like it.
That is where this becomes personal.
Because perhaps you are living in the uncomfortable distance between what God has promised and what you can currently see.
Abram knew that distance.
God had promised him descendants, yet years passed while the promise appeared biologically impossible.
Then Genesis 17 records something extraordinary.
God tells him:
“Neither shall thy name any more be called Abram, but thy name shall be Abraham.”
The Hebrew is striking:
וְלֹא־יִקָּרֵא עוֹד אֶת־שִׁמְךָ אַבְרָם וְהָיָה שִׁמְךָ אַבְרָהָם
V'lo-yikkare od et-shimkha Avram; v'hayah shimkha Avraham.
“No longer shall your name be called Abram; your name shall be Abraham.”
And God immediately connects the name with His covenant purpose: “for a father of many nations have I made thee.”
Notice the timing.
Isaac was not standing beside Abraham when God said it.
The house was not yet overflowing with descendants.
The nations were not visible.
Abraham was being required to carry a name connected to a promise he could not yet hold in his hands.
Imagine introducing yourself after that.
“What is your name?”
“Abraham.”
Father of a multitude.
And then the awkward silence.
“Where is the multitude?”
That is faith's uncomfortable territory.
God sometimes declares what His grace intends before circumstances display what His grace is accomplishing.
Then there was Jacob.
And Jacob's story is considerably messier.

His name, יַעֲקֹב — Ya'akov — is connected in Genesis with the heel, because he emerged from the womb holding Esau's heel. His life subsequently became marked by grasping, maneuvering, rivalry, deception, fear, and consequences.
He obtained Esau's birthright.
He deceived his father.
He fled from his brother.
He spent years dealing with Laban.
Eventually the man who had spent so much of his life maneuvering circumstances found himself alone in the darkness.
And there, beside the Jabbok, Jacob wrestled through the night.
Then came a question that sounds almost unnecessary.
“What is thy name?”
Jacob.
God knew his name.
The question forced Jacob to say it.
Jacob.
My history.
My reputation.
The identity attached to years of grasping.
Jacob had to bring his old name into the light before hearing what came next.
Then Genesis 32:28 says:
לֹא יַעֲקֹב יֵאָמֵר עוֹד שִׁמְךָ כִּי אִם־יִשְׂרָאֵל
Lo Ya'akov ye'amer od shimkha, ki im-Yisra'el...
“Your name shall no longer be called Jacob, but Israel...”
And Scripture continues:
כִּי־שָׂרִיתָ עִם־אֱלֹהִים וְעִם־אֲנָשִׁים וַתּוּכָל
Ki-sarita im-Elohim v'im-anashim vatukhal.
Because you have striven with God and with men and have prevailed.
“Israel” — יִשְׂרָאֵל, Yisra'el — is associated in the passage with striving or struggling with God.
But do not turn this into a sentimental slogan.
Jacob did not walk away untouched.
He walked away limping.
That may be one of the most beautiful details in the entire story.
The new name came with a limp.
Read that again.
The new name came with a limp.
God's transformation did not mean Jacob suddenly had no history.
It meant his history no longer possessed the authority to write the ending.
Maybe that is what somebody reading this desperately needs to understand.
Healing does not always erase the scar.
Grace does not mean you suddenly forget what happened.
Forgiveness does not make yesterday imaginary.
Sometimes redeemed people still limp.
Sometimes restored marriages carry scars.
Sometimes forgiven sinners remember exactly how low they fell.
Sometimes people who have been delivered still tremble when they tell the testimony.
But a scar is not the same thing as a sentence.
A limp is not the same thing as condemnation.
Your wound may explain part of your journey without being allowed to define your identity.
And then...
Simon walked into the presence of Jesus.
Before Simon had preached at Pentecost...
before thousands responded...
before the bold confession...
before the failures...
before the restoration...
before the leadership...
Jesus looked at him.
John preserves the moment in Greek:
Σὺ εἶ Σίμων... σὺ κληθήσῃ Κηφᾶς
Sy ei Simōn... sy klēthēsē Kēphas.
“You are Simon... you shall be called Cephas.”
John then explains:
ὃ ἑρμηνεύεται Πέτρος
ho hermēneuetai Petros —
“which is interpreted Peter.”
Κηφᾶς (Kēphas) represents the Aramaic Kepha, associated with rock; John supplies the Greek equivalent, Πέτρος (Petros).
Jesus was looking at Simon while speaking toward Peter.
Think about that.
Jesus saw what Simon currently was.
And Jesus knew what Simon would become.
But between those two realities there would be an enormous amount of failure.
Peter would speak too quickly.
Misunderstand Jesus.
Argue.
Boast.
Sink.
Sleep when he should pray.
Swing a sword when he should listen.
And then...
on the night Jesus was arrested...
Peter would deny Him.
Not once.
Three times.
The man Jesus had called toward “rock” would crumble under pressure.
A servant girl asks a question.
Peter retreats.
Another accusation.
Another denial.
Then another.
And according to Luke's Gospel, after the third denial, Jesus turned and looked at Peter.
Imagine that look.
The same Jesus who once looked at Simon and saw Peter...
now looked at Peter while Peter was behaving like the frightened man he thought he had outgrown.
Then the rooster crowed.
Peter remembered.
And he went outside and wept bitterly.
There are tears that come from getting caught.
And there are tears that come when you finally see what your sin has done.
Peter knew what Jesus had said.
Peter knew what Peter had promised.
And now Peter knew what Peter had done.
Maybe you know those tears.
You told God you would stop.
Then you went back.
You promised you would never open it again.
You opened it.
You promised you would forgive.
You became bitter again.
You said the relationship was over.
You returned.
You lifted your hands on Sunday while hiding something on Monday.
You told everyone, “I'm doing okay.”
But you weren't.
And perhaps somewhere inside you, another name began forming.
Fraud.
Hypocrite.
Disappointment.
Unworthy.
Too far gone.
Listen carefully.
Peter's denial was real.
Jesus never pretended otherwise.
Biblical grace never requires us to rename sin so that sinners can feel comfortable.
Sin is sin.
We have rebelled against a holy God.
We do not need improved self-esteem nearly as desperately as we need reconciliation with our Creator.
And that is exactly why the Gospel is so staggering.
Jesus knew about the courtyard before He called Simon Cephas.
Christ did not discover Peter's weakness when the rooster crowed.
He already knew.
He knew the boasting.
He knew the sleeping.
He knew the denial.
He knew the tears.
He knew the shame.
He knew the fishing boat Peter would eventually return to.
And Jesus went to the cross anyway.
That changes everything.
Christianity is not the story of bad people discovering better labels for themselves.
It is the announcement that the holy Son of God entered our ruined story, bore our sin, died in the place of sinners, and rose again victorious.
At the cross, Jesus did not excuse our scandal.
He carried its judgment.
“He was wounded for our transgressions.”
The innocent One stood where the guilty belonged.
The spotless Lamb bore sin.
The King wore thorns.
The Creator was mocked by His creatures.
The hands that formed humanity were pierced by human hands.
And from that apparent scandal came grace beyond comprehension.
Jesus died.
Jesus was buried.
Jesus rose.
And because Christ lives, repentance is not walking toward execution.
It is running toward mercy.
After the resurrection, Jesus went looking for Peter.
Not to pretend the denial never happened.
To restore him.
Three denials had filled Peter's memory.
Then, beside another charcoal fire, Jesus drew three declarations of love from him and repeatedly entrusted him with care for His sheep.
“Feed my sheep.”
Peter's worst chapter had not cancelled Christ's calling.
Grace did not tell Peter his denial was acceptable.
Grace transformed a denier into a shepherd.
That is the Gospel difference.
Grace does not merely make sinners feel better about remaining unchanged.
Grace forgives sinners and begins making them new.
And this is where the ancient stories stop feeling ancient.
Because perhaps nobody is going to change your legal name today.
But in Christ, something infinitely deeper can happen.
The New Testament speaks of those in Christ as a “new creation.”
Not improved ruins.
Not decorated graves.
New creation.
It says there is “now no condemnation to them which are in Christ Jesus.”
It says believers have received adoption.
It says we are forgiven according to the riches of His grace.
It says those who were once darkness are now “light in the Lord.”
The Gospel does not ask you to manufacture a heroic identity and repeat it until you believe it.
The Gospel gives you Christ.

And when you belong to Christ, your deepest identity is no longer determined by the ugliest thing you have done, the cruelest thing somebody has done to you, the addiction you battled, the relationship that collapsed, the person who abandoned you, or the season you wish you could erase.
Your sin must be confessed.
Your wounds may need healing.
Consequences may remain.
Reconciliation may require difficult obedience.
Repentance may cost you something.
But Jesus gets the final word.
That is why repentance is so beautiful.
Repentance is not God screaming, “Become worthy and then come home.”
You cannot make yourself worthy.
Repentance is turning from sin toward the Savior who already did what you could never do.
Maybe you have been carrying an old name for years.
Maybe your name is what your father called you when he was angry.
Maybe it is what the person who abused you made you believe about yourself.
Maybe it is what your divorce made you feel.
Maybe it is what your bank account says.
Maybe it is what pornography has whispered after another relapse.
Maybe it is what depression has whispered in a dark room.
Maybe it is what religious people called you after discovering your past.
Maybe it is simply the sentence you keep repeating:
“God could never use somebody like me.”
Peter might disagree.
Jacob might disagree.
Abraham might disagree.
And above all, the cross disagrees.
Because the cross is where every illusion of human righteousness dies...
and every hope of undeserved mercy becomes possible through Christ.
You do not need a new nickname.
You need a new heart.
You do not need to reinvent yourself.
You need Jesus.
You do not need to hide your scandal more effectively.
You need to bring it into the light of the Savior who already knows the whole story.
Confess.
Repent.
Come home.
Trust Christ.
Because Jesus specializes in walking into stories that look finished and writing resurrection where everybody else placed a period.
And maybe that is why you found this article today.
Not so you can merely say, “That was beautiful.”
But so you can answer a harder question.
What name have you been allowing your past to call you?
Be honest.
Somebody scrolling through the darkness tonight may need evidence that Christ is still restoring people.
Do not keep this article trapped on your screen.

Not because sharing a post earns God's favor. It does not. We are saved by grace, not social-media activity. But if this truth glorifies Christ, sharing it can become one small act of witness—placing the Gospel in front of someone who may never walk into your church but will stop long enough to read something you shared.
Send this to the believer quietly drifting away.
Send it to the friend ashamed to return to church.
Send it to the person who thinks Christianity is only for people who already have themselves together.
Because there may come a night when the old name starts whispering again.
And when it does, remember Jacob walking away with both a new name and a limp.
Remember Peter standing beside Jesus after denying Him.
Remember that grace does not erase the truth about your past.
Grace tells a greater truth about your future because of Christ.
If you want to support the mission and go deeper:
But before you leave, remember the question God asked Jacob in the darkness.
“What is your name?”
Maybe tonight it is time to stop answering with the name your shame gave you.
Not because you can rename yourself.
Not because positive thinking can redeem you.

But because Jesus Christ died and rose again so repentant sinners could be forgiven, reconciled to God, adopted into His family, transformed by His Spirit, and given a future their past could never manufacture.
Abram's circumstances did not get the final word.
Jacob's history did not get the final word.
Peter's denial did not get the final word.
And if you are in Christ...
your scandal does not get the final word either.
The rooster may remember the night you failed, but the empty tomb announces that Jesus is still writing your morning.
